planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February-April or September-November in deep shade with reliably moist soil. Moorblut is an older German-bred cultivar and the seed parent behind Britt-Marie Crawford, so it shares that dramatic dark foliage but is less commonly offered commercially. Give it a site near a pond edge, downspout, or other consistently damp spot, since it wilts hard in dry heat and Gulf Coast summers punish any lapse in watering.

directions: Moorblut is a dark-foliaged selection of Bigleaf Ligularia with rounded, coarsely toothed leaves that are dark brownish-green above and a contrasting deep purplish-brown beneath, an effect best appreciated where the undersides catch low light. From August into September it sends up branching stems topped with large, light orange daisy flowers that stand out sharply against the somber foliage and draw bees heavily. Grow it in cool, evenly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since like all bigleaf ligularias it collapses visibly within hours of drying out. As one of the parents of the popular 'Britt-Marie Crawford', it offers a similar look for gardeners hunting a less ubiquitous alternative.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Ligularia dentata
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ligularia

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall into consistently moist to boggy soil; site in the coolest, shadiest, dampest spot available since this is one of the largest-growing ligularias and needs ample soil moisture to support its bulk. In hot zone 9 gardens treat it as a bog-margin or pondside specimen rather than a border plant.

directions: Wilson's Ligularia is a bold, large-growing species with broad, coarsely serrated, forest-green rounded leaves and tightly packed, upright spikes of small yellow daisy flowers that rise well above the foliage from early to midsummer. It grows considerably taller than the more familiar Ligularia dentata cultivars, reaching four to six feet in bloom, and makes a strong architectural statement at the back of a moist shade border or along a stream or pond margin. It prefers partial shade to light shade with rich, consistently moist to wet soil and will even tolerate periods of standing water, but like other ligularias it wilts quickly if the soil dries out. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Ligularia wilsoniana
Kew Science, Plants of the World Online — Ligularia wilsoniana

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in dappled or partial shade; choose a site sheltered from cold winter wind, as this species is slower and more temperamental to establish than the more common Florida anise.

directions: A rare Chinese and Himalayan species distinct from the familiar Gulf Coast anise shrubs, Illicium simonsii bears leathery, glossy, dark green lance-shaped leaves and unusual pale yellow, fragrant flowers in mid- to late summer rather than the maroon or white spring blooms typical of Illicium floridanum. It grows slowly into a dense, rounded evergreen shrub and rewards patience with a distinctive flowering season that extends the anise-shrub display later into the year. Site it in a warm but sheltered position with dappled shade and well-drained, acidic soil, and protect it from hard freezes and drying winter wind until well established, as it is less reliably cold-hardy than eastern Illicium species. As with all anise shrubs, crushed foliage is aromatic but all plant parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online — Illicium simonsii

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, organically rich, neutral to acidic soil in partial shade to full shade; it tolerates more sun than other anise shrubs if soil moisture stays high, and performs well in the same shaded, damp sites favored by Illicium floridanum.

directions: Native to China, this erect, narrow anise tree produces simple, leathery, anise-scented leaves and unusual light pink to orange-pink, waxy, star-shaped flowers, followed by star-shaped seed capsules with ten to thirteen follicles, more than the eight typical of true star anise. It grows taller and narrower than the Gulf Coast Illicium species, making it useful as a narrow evergreen screen or vertical accent at the back of a shaded, moist border. Give it consistently moist to wet, organically rich, neutral-to-acidic soil, and it is notably deer resistant, an asset in woodland plantings where deer pressure limits other shrub choices. Despite the common name referencing anise, no part of this species is edible and all parts are toxic if ingested, unlike the culinary star anise, Illicium verum.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Illicium lanceolatum
Trees and Shrubs Online — Illicium lanceolatum
